lead: ARM7TDMI is the classic 32-bit core in older microcontrollers. Cortex-M is the family in most new ones. The two share the ARM programmer's model, so one compiler toolchain, with a different target option, serves either. They differ in pipeline, bus structure and interrupt hardware. Choosing a chip for a smart meter, a motor drive or a washing machine starts here.
prereq: You need: load-store RISC and the ARM families from 6.1, registers and CPSR from 6.2, exceptions from 6.3, Thumb from 6.5, and pipelining from Unit 1.

blocks.text: ARM7TDMI is a 32-bit load-store RISC core. Each letter names a feature: T is Thumb, D is debug, M is the enhanced multiplier, I is the EmbeddedICE debug unit. Only a few universities teach it in detail today, yet it sits inside many older microcontrollers.

items: Fetch reads the next instruction from memory.
Decode reads the instruction fetched one cycle earlier.
Execute runs the instruction fetched two cycles earlier.
A taken branch discards the two younger instructions and refills the pipeline, costing extra cycles.

blocks.text: One 32-bit bus carries both instructions and data, so the core is von Neumann, not Harvard (Unit 1). Load and store are the only instructions that touch memory. Arithmetic works on registers R0 to R15, but R13 is the stack pointer, R14 the link register and R15 the program counter, so ordinary data processing mostly uses R0 to R12. Thumb gives 16-bit encodings of common instructions, as 6.5 explains, so code fits in smaller flash.

Cortex-M cores target microcontrollers. M0 and M0+ are the smallest; M3 and M4 add speed, and M4 adds DSP instructions. The programmer's model is still 6.2: sixteen registers, a status register, Thread and Handler modes.

The NVIC (Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller) sits inside the core. Each interrupt has a vector address, an enable bit and a priority; a higher priority pre-empts a running handler. Tail-chaining moves from one handler to the next without unwinding, and late arrival lets a higher-priority request start first. On M3 and M4 the delay from interrupt request to the first handler instruction is a fixed 12 cycles.

M3 and M4 have separate instruction and data buses (Harvard) joined by a bus matrix, so a fetch and a load overlap. They run Thumb-2: 16-bit instructions for density plus 32-bit ones for wide constants. M0 and M0+ implement ARMv6-M, a cut-down Thumb-2 subset. It is mostly 16-bit instructions with a few 32-bit ones (BL, MSR, MRS, DMB, DSB, ISB). IT blocks, CBZ, hardware divide and the wider data-processing instructions are missing, so code built for an M3 does not run on an M0 unchanged. M0/M0+ suit sensors and toys, M3/M4 motor drives, meters and medical devices, and ARM7TDMI older designs that add an external interrupt controller.

figure.caption: Two core families side by side: the classic core, and the microcontroller core with its built-in NVIC and, on M3 and M4, Harvard buses and Thumb-2.

spec.aria: Core comparison tree: ARM7TDMI uses a 3-stage von Neumann design with Thumb, while Cortex-M adds the NVIC and, on M3 and M4, Harvard buses and Thumb-2.

examples.question: An ARM7TDMI three-stage pipeline (fetch, decode, execute) takes one clock cycle per stage. Five independent instructions enter back to back, the first in cycle 1. (a) In which cycle does the fifth finish? (b) How long would the same five take on a non-pipelined core needing three cycles per instruction? (c) What is the speedup?
steps: With no stalls, instruction i is fetched in cycle i, decoded in cycle i+1 and executed in cycle i+2.
Instruction 1 finishes in cycle 3. Instruction 5 is fetched in cycle 5 and finishes in cycle 7, so the run costs 7 cycles.
examples.answer: The fifth instruction finishes in cycle 7, against 15 cycles without pipelining, a speedup of 2.14.
examples.check:
n = 5
stages = 3
pipelined = n + stages - 1
plain = n * stages
speedup = round(plain / pipelined, 2)
print(pipelined)
print(plain)
print(speedup)

traps: T in ARM7TDMI means Thumb, not Thumb-2. Thumb-2 arrives with later architectures and the Cortex-M3.
The ARM7TDMI has one memory bus, so it is von Neumann at core level. The Harvard label belongs to Cortex-M3 and M4, not to every ARM chip.
The NVIC is part of the Cortex-M core and is memory-mapped, not an external controller like the 8259 of Unit 5.
Pipelining raises throughput, not the speed of one instruction, which still spends three cycles in the pipeline.

M0 and M0+ implement ARMv6-M, a cut-down Thumb-2 subset: mostly 16-bit instructions plus a few 32-bit ones (BL, MSR, MRS, DMB, DSB, ISB). IT blocks, CBZ, hardware divide and the wider data-processing instructions are missing, so code built for an M3 does not run on an M0 unchanged.

quiz.q: Name the three ARM7TDMI pipeline stages.
ARM is a RISC design, yet the ARM7TDMI is called von Neumann. Explain both labels.
quiz.a: RISC describes the instruction set: load-store, fixed length. Von Neumann describes the single shared bus that carries both instructions and data.

quiz.q: Why does a fixed 12-cycle interrupt latency help a motor-control program?
quiz.a: The response time to every interrupt is the same known 12 cycles, so the worst-case loop timing can be worked out on paper and the sampling instant stays fixed. A variable latency would make the loop jitter and could break the motor current control.

quiz.q: Six independent instructions run on a three-stage ARM7TDMI pipeline, the first fetched in cycle 1. In which cycle does the sixth finish?
A product needs 40 interrupt sources and 32-bit immediate constants. Pick ARM7TDMI or Cortex-M3 and justify with two points.
quiz.a: Cortex-M3. Its NVIC handles up to 240 sources with built-in priority, and Thumb-2 gives 32-bit instructions with wide immediates. The ARM7TDMI would need an external controller and has no Thumb-2.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cortex-M4F adds floating point, Cortex-M7 adds caches and dual-issue, and Cortex-M23/M33 bring ARMv8-M TrustZone security for firmware updates and payment terminals. Vendor tools and CMSIS core headers start from exactly this NVIC and Thumb-2 model.
